final.answer: Yes, FV-104-2 can be supplied with flanged ends. Per its datasheet (Fisher ET, Table 3 'Available Constructions', p. 5), flanged options include CL125 FF (cast iron only), CL250 RF (cast iron), and RF or RTJ flanged CL150/CL300/CL600 for steel bodies; EN flanged connections to EN1092-1/B in PN16–PN100 are also available for metric sizes. Butt weld and screwed connections are also offered (screwed only for NPS 1, 1-1/2 and 2 on ET/ETR), plus socket weld on steel bodies. The exact combination depends on valve type, size and body material per Table 3.

Its datasheet (Fisher ET/D100022X012, Table 14, p. 20–21) lists the following valve plug seal materials and temperature limits: Carbon-filled PTFE, –73 to 232 °C (–100 to 450 °F), standard for NPS 1–6 except Cavitrol III cages; Ethylene-propylene, –40 to 232 °C (–40 to 450 °F), good for hot water/steam but not petroleum-based fluids; Fluorocarbon, –18 to 204 °C (0 to 400 °F), not for steam or ammonia; Nitrile, –40 to 71 °C (–40 to 160 °F) for air/hydrocarbons or up to 82 °C (180 °F) for other fluids. Alternatively, a spring-loaded plug seal is available: PTFE with N10276 spring, –73 to 232 °C (–100 to 450 °F), and PTFE/graphite with R30003 spring (with PEEK anti-extrusion rings), –73 to 316 °C (–100 to 600 °F), limited to 260 °C (500 °F) in oxidizing service. PEEK anti-extrusion rings are listed as not limiting for temperature (extended limit 316 °C / 600 °F non-oxidizing, 260 °C / 500 °F oxidizing). {"tool": "datasheet", "tag": "FV-106-2", "question": "Which seal or piston ring materials are available, and what temperatures are they good for?"}

Tool result:
Datasheet fisher-et-d100022x012, pages [20, 21, 2]:
Answering from Table 14 "Materials and Temperature Limits for Other Parts", page 20 of the datasheet (with notes on page 21) [p. 20, p. 21].

The valve plug seal (the seal ring between the plug and the seat) is available with these soft seal materials:

- **Carbon-filled PTFE**: –73 °C to 232 °C (–100 °F to 450 °F). Standard for NPS 1 thru 6 valves except those with Cavitrol III cages [p. 20].
- **Ethylene-propylene**: –40 °C to 232 °C (–40 °F to 450 °F). Excellent resistance to hot water and steam and most fire-resistant hydraulic oils, but cannot be used with petroleum-based fluids and other hydrocarbons [p. 20].
- **Fluorocarbon**: –18 °C to 204 °C (0 °F to 400 °F). For high-temperature air, hydrocarbons and certain other chemicals and solvents; not for use with steam or ammonia, and not recommended for water above 82 °C / 180 °F [p. 20, p. 21].
- **Nitrile**: –40 °C to 71 °C (–40 °F to 160 °F) for use with air and hydrocarbons, or up to 82 °C (180 °F) for other compatible fluids. Cannot be used with fire-resistant hydraulic oils [p. 20].

Alternatively, a **spring-loaded valve plug seal** is available:
- **PTFE with N10276 spring**: –73 °C to 232 °C (–100 °F to 450 °F). Standard for the NPS 8 valve regardless of cage, and for all NPS 1 thru 6 valves with Cavitrol III cages; optional in NPS 1 thru 6 valves with other cages [p. 20].
- **PTFE/graphite with R30003 spring** (for applications using PEEK anti-extrusion rings): –73 °C to 316 °C (–100 °F to 600 °F), and up to 260 °C / 500 °F for oxidizing service [p. 20, p. 21].
- The spring/retaining hardware can be S30200, S31600, or S41600 stainless steel (S41600 limited to –29 °C / –20 °F minimum); these metal parts are listed as "not limiting factors" for temperature. Note: these parts are not used with ports of 137 mm / 7 in. or larger [p. 20, p. 21].

Also available for seal applications: **PEEK** (PolyEtherEtherKetone) anti-extrusion rings — listed as "not limiting" for temperature [p. 20]. For extended-temperature (ET) constructions with PEEK anti-extrusion rings, the datasheet lists an extended limit of 316 °C / 600 °F in non-oxidizing service and 260 °C / 500 °F in oxidizing service [p. 2].

I could not find in these facts any part called a "piston ring" — the datasheet covers valve plug seal rings, anti-extrusion rings, retaining rings, and similar; if you meant a different part, it is not covered here.

final.answer: The transmitter feeding FIC-10-2 is FT-10-2 (a Rosemount 3051 measuring flow from pump P-10-1). Its failure direction is not fixed — it is user-selectable. On a detected sensor or microprocessor failure, the 4-20 mA output is driven either high or low depending on a jumper/switch setting on the transmitter; the standard configuration default is Alarm = High (≥ 21.75 mA, or ≥ 22.5 mA in the NAMUR-compliant setting; low alarm ≤ 3.75 mA, or ≤ 3.6 mA NAMUR; custom levels 20.2–23.0 mA high / 3.6–3.8 mA low). To change the direction, set the internal jumper/switch on the transmitter, or specify it at ordering time via option codes (C4 = NAMUR high, CN = NAMUR low, CR = custom high, CS = custom low, CT = Rosemount standard low; alarm-level options apply only to the HART 4-20 mA output code A). The datasheet does not contain the step-by-step procedure for changing the jumper on the unit itself.

trace.content: Consider the transmitter that feeds controller FIC-10-2. When the transmitter fails, does the output go high or low, and how do I change that alarm direction?
{"tool": "drawing", "question": "Which transmitter (FT tag) feeds controller FIC-10-2, and what does it measure?"}

Tool result:
{"answer": "Transmitter FT-10-2 sends its signal to controller FIC-10-2. FT-10-2 measures pump P-10-1, so the loop monitors the flow produced by centrifugal pump P-10-1.", "not_present": false}
{"tool": "datasheet", "tag": "FT-10-2", "question": "On signal failure, does the transmitter output fail high or low, and how is the alarm direction (high/low) configured or changed?"}

Tool result:
Datasheet rosemount-3051-00813-0100-4001, pages [88, 26, 63, 42, 74, 15, 52, 85]:
**Short answer:** It can fail either high or low — you choose the direction with a jumper/switch on the transmitter. On failure, the output goes to an alarm level that depends on which alarm setting (default, NAMUR-compliant, or custom) the transmitter is configured to.

**Details for HART 4-20 mA output (option code A)** [p. 88, Table 5: Failure mode alarm]:
- If self-diagnostics detect a sensor or microprocessor failure, the analog signal is driven either high or low to alert the user.
- **High or low failure mode is user-selectable with a jumper/switch on the transmitter.**
- The failure-mode alarm levels are:
  - **Default setting:** high alarm ≥ 21.75 mA (footnote: ≥ 22.5 mA for some options — codes M6, DA1, T9, RK); low alarm ≤ 3.75 mA.
  - **NAMUR-compliant setting:** high alarm ≥ 22.5 mA; low alarm ≤ 3.6 mA.
  - **Custom levels:** high alarm 20.2–23.0 mA; low alarm 3.6–3.8 mA. Footnote: the low alarm must be 0.1 mA less than the low saturation level and the high alarm must be 0.1 mA greater than the high saturation level.

**If your transmitter is a 1-5 Vdc low-power output (code M)** [p. 88]:
- On gross failure the signal is driven below 0.94 V (low alarm) or above 5.4 V (high alarm).
- The high or low alarm signal is user-selectable by an internal jumper.

**If your transmitter is output code F, W, or X (digital protocols such as FOUNDATION Fieldbus)** [p. 88]: there is no high/low analog alarm signal; instead, a gross transmitter failure is passed as an alert and a status together with the process variable.

**Ordering the alarm level** [pp. 15, 26, 42, 52, 63, 74]: the alarm direction/levels can also be set at ordering time via option codes — C4 = NAMUR high alarm, CN = NAMUR low alarm, CR = custom high alarm, CS = custom low alarm, CT = Rosemount standard low alarm. Note: the alarm levels option is only available with HART 4-20 mA output (code A). The standard configuration default is Alarm = High (not applicable to FOUNDATION Fieldbus, PROFIBUS PA, or wireless) [p. 109].

I could not find in these facts the exact step-by-step procedure for changing the jumper/switch setting on the transmitter itself.

cypher:
MATCH (a:PlantItem {tag: 'P-43-3'}), (b:PlantItem {tag: 'TV-316-2'})
MATCH p = shortestPath((a)-[:line_to*]->(b))
WITH [n IN nodes(p) | n.tag] AS tags
RETURN tags

MATCH (a:PlantItem {tag: 'P-43-3'})
MATCH (a)-[:line_to*1..]->(d:PlantItem)
RETURN DISTINCT d.tag AS tag, d.kind AS kind
ORDER BY tag

MATCH (tv:PlantItem {tag: 'TV-316-2'})
MATCH p = shortestPath((src:PlantItem)-[:line_to*1..]->(tv))
WHERE src.no_inflow = true
RETURN [n IN nodes(p) | n.tag] AS upstream_path_tags

MATCH (tv:PlantItem {tag: 'TV-316-2'})
OPTIONAL MATCH (up:PlantItem)-[:line_to]->(tv)
OPTIONAL MATCH (tv)-[:line_to]->(down:PlantItem)
RETURN 'upstream' AS direction, up.tag AS tag, up.no_inflow AS no_inflow, up.no_outflow AS no_outflow
UNION
MATCH (tv:PlantItem {tag: 'TV-316-2'})
OPTIONAL MATCH (down:PlantItem)<-[:line_to]-(tv)
RETURN 'downstream' AS direction, down.tag AS tag, down.no_inflow AS no_inflow, down.no_outflow AS no_outflow

MATCH (v:PlantItem {tag: 'TV-316-2'})
OPTIONAL MATCH (u:PlantItem)-[r1:line_to]->(v)
OPTIONAL MATCH (v)-[r2:line_to]->(d:PlantItem)
RETURN CASE WHEN r1 IS NOT NULL THEN u.tag END AS upstream_tag,
       CASE WHEN r2 IS NOT NULL THEN d.tag END AS downstream_tag
ORDER BY upstream_tag, downstream_tag
